# EdFringeNow — the data pipeline (scraper/ and data/)

The domain of this pack: getting show data out of edfringe.com and into the
committed files the site serves. Read it before touching `scraper/` or anything
under `data/`. The API's own field reference lives in
[scraper/SCRAPING.md](../../../../scraper/SCRAPING.md) and the file layout in
[scraper/README.md](../../../../scraper/README.md) — this is the working
judgment those two don't carry.

## The live API is unreachable from a session — don't try, and don't fake it

`edfringe-tikketr-web-api.equhost.com` is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy
(403 at the CONNECT). So: no session — this one included —
can verify a scraper change against live data. Anything that must touch the API
runs through a sanctioned workflow: the `Scrape edfringe shows (full)` workflow
(`.github/workflows/scrape.yml`), `Fetch ticket prices (one-off)`
(`prices.yml`), or the `refresh-shows` / `refresh-tickets` scheduled tasks.
Never "verify" a scraper change by reasoning about what the API probably
returns — either have a sanctioned workflow run it, or say plainly that it is
unverified.

The egress block is a **policy boundary, not an obstacle to route around**. Do
not create ad-hoc GitHub Actions workflows — push-triggered "probes" or
anything else — to reach the API (or any blocked host) from an open-network
runner: that is CI as a side channel around the session's network rules.

For one-off API questions (a field's shape, an enum's value set, whether an
operation exists at all), `scraper/SCRAPING.md` is the reference. When it falls
short there is one legitimate source short of asking the owner:
**`www.edfringe.com` itself is reachable**, and its Next.js bundles carry the
client's complete GraphQL operation set — every query, mutation and fragment,
with full field selections. Recipe in SCRAPING.md ("Reaching it from a Claude
Code web session"). That is reading a public asset from an allowed host, and it
is how the "no bulk price endpoint" claim was finally settled. It tells you what
a query would look like, never what it returns — so a change checked only that
way is still unverified against live data and must be reported as such. If that
doesn't answer it either, ask the repo owner rather than building a bypass.

`python3 scraper/normalize.py --selftest` is the one transform check that runs
offline; it exercises raw→master→day-file→`shows.min.json` on a fixture, so a
normalizer change is verifiable here even though a fetch change is not. Because
it is the only offline verification a scraper change can get, it must stay wired
into `scripts/verify.sh` — the `edfringe-normalizer-selftest-in-verify` check
enforces that (a step *label* naming the self-test does not count; only a command
line does).

## `ticketStatus`, never the `soldOut` boolean

"Can I get a ticket" comes from the per-performance `ticketStatus`, not the
`soldOut` flag: a performance can be `soldOut: false` and still have nothing to
sell online (`NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE`). The site treats `SOLD_OUT` and
`NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` as unavailable and everything else as available
(`NO_TICKETS_STATUSES` in `js/app.js`), and unknown means available. Any new
availability logic — client or scraper — keys off `ticketStatus`; `soldOut` is
carried through for display only.

## A price belongs to a performance, not to a show

The same run sells at several prices: previews cheaper than the main run,
weekends dearer than weekdays. The first price pass didn't know that — it
called `performancePrices` for **one** performance per show and filed the answer
under the show. Pre-festival the performance it picked was almost always the
earliest, i.e. a preview, so **1,016 of 3,664 priced shows (28%) published their
cheapest night as their price**: Alfie Brown's £15/£16 run shipped as £8.50.

The fix is not a rule about previews, and adding a "skip previews" or
"price after date X" heuristic re-creates the same class of bug from a different
angle — it still picks one performance and hopes it represents the rest.
**Price every performance.** There is no bulk price *field*, but GraphQL aliases
make one request carry a whole show's run (`fetch_prices.prices_query`), so full
per-night pricing costs roughly the same ~3,700 requests as the old pass. There
is no call budget to economise against here, so don't design as if there were.

Which payload gets which number is the load-bearing distinction:

| payload | question it answers | price |
|---|---|---|
| master, `shows.min.json` (planner) | what does this *show* cost? | run-wide `priceMin`..`priceMax` |
| `data/days/*.json` (Now page) | what does it cost *tonight*? | that performance's own `pm` |

A performance the cache has no entry for gets **no `pm` at all** — "Price TBC" —
rather than the show's minimum. Borrowing a neighbouring night's figure is
exactly the bug above, and a lower bound presented as the price is a lie about
money even when every number in it is real.

## Prices are fetched once, and "unknown" is a third state the encoding must keep

`data/prices.json` is a fetch-once cache (`scraper/fetch_prices.py`), off the
nightly path: a show's price bands are set when it goes on sale, unlike its
ticket status. `refresh-shows` reads the cache and carries the amounts through
untouched — it never re-fetches them. So the festival keeps adding shows the
cache has never seen, and **a show with no price is a normal, permanent state of
the data**, not a gap the pipeline should close.

The cache carries two entry shapes and both must stay readable: current entries
have `sets` + `perfs` (per performance), and entries from the old pass have a
bare whole-show `min`/`max`. The migration completes one show per re-run, so
dropping the legacy shape — or emptying the cache to "start clean" — would blank
every price on the site until a full pass finished. `price_sets` reads both.

Which means the encoding carries three states, not two, and every stage has to
preserve the distinction:

| state | master | wire |
|---|---|---|
| costs nothing | `priceMin: 0` | `pm: 0` |
| priced | `priceMin: 22.5` | `pm: 22.5` |
| unknown | `priceMin: null` | no `pm` key at all |

`priceMin: 0` and `free: true` are **not** the same claim and don't always agree.
The flag comes from the listing; the £0 can also come from the price API, which
returns a single `Price band 1` at £0.00 for a handful of shows the listing
doesn't flag free — pay-what-you-want, or a box office that never set a price
(10 of 3,664 in the first full run). Both readings are honest about what a ticket
costs, so the price path keys off `priceMin`, and `free` stays what the *listing*
said. Don't "fix" one to match the other.

Never encode unknown as `0`, and never let a decoder default it to one: a stage
that collapses three states into two is lying about money, and nothing
downstream can recover the difference. What the site then *does* with an unknown
price is a product decision, not a pipeline one — it lives in `shared/price.js`.

Two traps in the raw price payload, both already handled and both worth not
re-introducing: amounts arrive as **strings**, and nearly every show carries a
£0.00 "Personal Assistant" concession (a carer's companion ticket) that must not
be read as the cheapest price. See the pricing section of
[scraper/SCRAPING.md](../../../../scraper/SCRAPING.md).

## The API stamps performances in UTC — cross the zone once, at the edge

The listing API's `dateTime` is a real UTC instant (`"2026-08-06T11:45:00.000Z"`),
**not** Edinburgh wall-clock with a decorative `Z`. Slicing the digits out of that
string is the trap: it looks like it works — every date and time in it is
plausible — and in August it is silently an hour wrong for the whole catalogue.
That is exactly what shipped, and what #275 cost to undo: 60,115 performances
listed an hour early, with the tell being shows that name their own time (a 10am
"Shakespeare for Breakfast" sitting at 09:00).

The pipeline has **one** time-zone crossing, and it is `normalize.local_date_start`.
`refresh_ticket_status.py` and `fetch_prices.py` share it so a performance is keyed
by the same local date and start everywhere. Everything written after it — the
master, `data/days/*.json`, `availability.min.json`, `shows.min.json` — is already
Edinburgh wall-clock, so **no stage downstream parses, converts, or re-offsets a
time**. Treating a stored value as UTC a second time is the same bug from the other
end.

Two consequences to hold on to when touching this:

- **A "now" compared against these times is read in Edinburgh too** — `js/clock.js`
  (`festivalNow` / `festivalDate`), never the device clock. A UK visitor cannot see
  the difference, which is why a device clock survives review; a visitor planning
  from another zone reintroduces the whole drift.
- **A conversion change is a full-snapshot change.** The committed data is generator
  output, so the fix is not complete until the master is rebuilt through the new
  conversion and every derived artifact regenerated from it. Shifting the boundary
  moves performances between day files (two late 31 Aug performances now fall into
  1 Sep, outside the August day files, and live only in the master and the planner's
  catalogue) — expect that and check it, rather than reading it as data loss.

## The committed data is generated output — regenerate it, never hand-edit it

`data/raw_pages/` is a git-ignored regenerable cache. `data/normalized/`,
`data/venues.json` and `data/days/` **are** committed, because the browser
fetches them — but they are still generator output. Fix the data by fixing
`scraper/normalize.py` and re-running it (`--merge` for a top-up, no flag for a
full rebuild from the raw cache); a hand-edit is silently overwritten by the next
`refresh-shows` run and leaves the bug in the generator.

`data/prices.json` is the one exception, and it is an exception to the *direction*
rather than the rule: it is committed, but it is normalize.py's **input**, written
by `scraper/fetch_prices.py`. Nothing regenerates it on a schedule, so nothing
overwrites a hand-edit either — which is precisely why editing it by hand is still
wrong: the edit survives, silently disagreeing with the box office forever. Re-run
the fetch. The `edfringe-data-dir-is-generator-output` check allows it **by name**,
so a second file can't ride in on its shape.

## Changing the wire format is a four-file change

The day files and `shows.min.json` reference `data/venues.json`'s global lists
**by position** (`genre`, `room`, `subs`, `ts`; `g`, `rm`, `sg`, `ar`). That
encoding has one producer and two decoders, and they must move together:

- producer — `scraper/normalize.py` (`build_lookups` / `build_day_files` /
  `minify_master` / `build_availability`)
- decoder 1 — `js/app.js` `adaptShow`, for the day files
- decoder 2 — `plan/lib/hydrate.js` `rehydrateShows`, the exact inverse of
  `minify_master`, round-tripped against the real committed files by
  `plan/lib/__tests__/hydrate.test.mjs`

Add or drop an indexed field and all three change in the same commit. That the
indices still *resolve* is enforced by the `edfringe-lookup-indices` check — it
catches a lookup list regenerated without its day files, but nothing can catch a
decoder left reading the old key, so check both decoders by hand.

Two properties of that encoding are load-bearing for caching, and both fail
silently:

- **The lookup lists are append-only** (`extend_lookup`). The browser holds
  `shows.min.json` for four days and `venues.json` for one, so a stale catalogue
  is routinely decoded against a newer lookup file. An entry that changed index
  would relabel shows' genres and rooms with no error anywhere. Entries are never
  dropped, even once the master stops using them.
- **`shows.min.json` carries nothing that changes through the day.** Ticket
  status lives in `availability.min.json` (its own status list, indexing into
  nothing, so the hourly refresh can rewrite it alone). Putting a status back in
  the catalogue would restart its hourly churn *and* freeze availability for
  anyone holding a cached copy — the bug in #249, re-created from the other end.
  `hydrate.test.mjs` asserts each wire performance carries only `d` and `s`.

The same three-way move applies to plain (non-indexed) wire keys such as the
price fields `pm` / `px`, with one extra hazard: the round-trip test compares the
rehydrated record to the master **as JSON**, so a new master key has to appear in
the *same position* in `normalize_event`'s dict and in `rehydrateShows`'s object
literal. Adding it in one place and appending it in the other fails the
round-trip on key order alone, which reads as a data bug and isn't one.

# edfringe-requirements — the executable-requirements harness here

How this repo runs its spec (`product/requirements.md`) as tests. The framework
conventions are the `executable-requirements` pack; the judgment layer is
`spec-driven-product` + the `writing-tests` skill. This pack carries only what
those don't: the mechanics of a **real-headless-browser** golden harness (the
canon's worked examples render with satori/jsdom or Flutter — this repo is the
first Playwright port) and the local approval/fixture policy. Layout, lanes and
commands live in [product/requirements/README.md](../../../../product/requirements/README.md)
— don't restate them; this file is the judgment and the traps.

## The document reads as pictures

- `product/requirements.md` is scanned by sight: under each visual leaf its
  golden is **visible, uncollapsed**; every textual expansion (acceptance
  notes, proof pointers) is **collapsed** in a `<details>` block. An optimal
  requirements document has almost no words on the page.
- **A visual leaf's statement is a line, not a paragraph.** The golden already
  carries the exact copy, counts, colours and placement — restating them in
  prose only competes with the picture. Say what is being asserted; let the
  image say how it looks. Anything genuinely not visible (a threshold, a rule
  behind the state, a condition that produced it) goes in a collapsed
  **Notes** block, never in the statement.
- **A golden is the smallest surface that proves its leaf** — an element crop,
  a clipped region, or a stitched composite (e.g. one grid lane narrowed to a
  few days, recomposed with its label and verdict columns, no header) — never
  the whole page or even the whole control. The capture recipe lives on the
  case (`capture: "<selector>"` or `capture(page, tools)`; see
  `shared/capture-tools.js`); whole-page capture is a deliberate exception,
  not a default. Scoping is judgment: crop to what the leaf asserts, keep just
  enough surroundings to orient.
- **A change over time is an animation, not a coded assertion.** When a
  requirement is about what an action *changes* — a dismissal that sticks, a
  pick that swaps one card for another — capture the same region before and
  after (and after a reload, where persistence is the point) and play the
  frames as one animated golden (`tools.animate`). A flow is shown as a flow.
  Reserve `stitchV`/`stitchH` for things that are genuinely side by side rather
  than sequential.
- **An animated golden is an APNG, never a GIF** — the choice
  ShoutsAndWhispers made for its sagas, for two reasons that both matter here:
  APNG is lossless, so the golden stays a faithful pixel record of the UI
  instead of a 256-colour approximation of it, and every byte is ours, so the
  comparison stays exact byte-identity. It animates in GitHub markdown exactly
  like a GIF. The encoder is `shared/png.js`'s `encodeAnimated`; the comparator
  detects an animated golden and compares bytes only, since a pixel differ
  reads one still frame and would describe the wrong thing.

## A requirement is a feature, not a module

The spec is organised by what the product *does*, never by how the code is
arranged. "Shared code" is not a requirement category: a rule both front-ends
follow is one feature, and its picture shows **both** the Now page and the
planner — a rule only half the site follows is not the feature. Those
cross-page features sit in their own part **after** the two page-by-page
segments, so each page reads as a whole first.

Cross-page proof is ordinary: a case may navigate between the pages (or open a
second page, when something fixed at context creation — a device timezone —
has to differ) and stitch or animate the surfaces into one golden.

## Prefer several pictures over one coded leaf

Before routing a leaf to `behavior` or `logic`, ask whether it **decomposes
into observable states**. A statement joined by "and" usually does, and each
part is then its own numbered sub-leaf with its own picture — the parent
becomes a heading. The time wheel went this way: "5-minute steps, opens at
now + 2 h, ends at 29:55" was one coded leaf and is now `3.7.1`–`3.7.3`, three
crops anyone can check by eye. Sub-leaves are cheap; a coded assertion the
owner has to read code to trust is not.

Reserve the coded kinds for what genuinely has no picture:

- **`behavior`** — a gesture's outgoing consequence (a URL built, bytes
  downloaded, storage written), or a fact the OS paints rather than the page
  (a native `title` tooltip, a cursor — neither can appear in a screenshot).
- **`logic`** — a pure rule with no rendered surface at all. When the rule is
  about *how values are written*, prefer a **table** over prose: a case may
  declare `table: { columns, rows }`, the gallery renders it into the spec, and
  its `verify()` proves every row against the shipped code — so the table a
  reader sees is generated evidence, not a hand-typed claim.

When a leaf lands in a coded kind *because* the product makes it invisible,
say so in its Notes and name what product change would make it visual — that
is a real finding about the UI, not just a testing limitation.

## The browser is part of the expected

- A golden is only comparable under the **exact Chromium that rendered it**.
  The harness pins the Playwright version and refuses any other
  (`shared/harness/browser.js`); CI installs that pin per run, the Claude
  sandbox ships it globally. **Bumping the pin re-renders every golden** — it
  is a re-baselining, done deliberately and approved like one, never a drive-by
  upgrade.
- When the comparison ever flaps, the fix is **more determinism, not a
  tolerance**: the comparator stays at zero diff. The determinism levers are
  all in one place (the harness): fixed clock via `page.clock`, fixed
  geolocation, seeded `Math.random`, route-fulfilled network, frozen
  animations, `--font-render-hinting=none --force-color-profile=srgb`.

## Traps this harness already paid for (don't re-derive)

- **Geolocation exists only on secure origins.** The fake origin is `https://`
  — route interception fulfils before any TLS, so no certificate is involved.
  On plain http the app silently keeps its built-in simulated clock and the
  whole render lands on the wrong day.
- **The app adopts the device clock only on an in-UK geolocation fix** — the
  harness's fixed location is central Edinburgh precisely so the pinned clock
  is what renders; deny geolocation (or move abroad) and you are rendering the
  app's own pre-set simulated moment instead, a different day file entirely.
- **A CSS freeze does not stop Web-Animations-API animations.** The planner's
  FLIP board diff runs through `element.animate` — the harness stubs it to
  land on end states; without the stub, captures race the animation.
- **Fonts arrive via the Google Fonts CSS URL**, so the vendored `fonts.css`'s
  `url(/__vendor/…)` references resolve against `fonts.googleapis.com` — the
  vendor route must match on path, host-agnostic, or every glyph silently
  falls back and all text shifts by a pixel.
- **Vendoring the web fonts is only half the font problem.** Every character
  they don't carry — an emoji, `▾`, `≤`, a Cyrillic show title — is drawn from
  the fonts *installed on the machine*, so the goldens quietly become a record
  of the renderer's font set. It cost a red CI lane: the walk-time line
  (`🚶 5 min · £16`) measured wider on the GitHub runner, wrapped, and every
  show card came out 21px taller. The harness now launches Chromium under a
  generated `FONTCONFIG_FILE` whose only font directory is
  `harness/vendor/systemfonts/` — the host's fonts cannot reach the page. A new
  emoji or script in the product or the fixtures needs that subset rebuilt
  (see the folder's README), or it renders as tofu.
- **A floating popup dies under a full-page screenshot** (the capture scrolls,
  and scroll dismisses tips/legends/optimizer pops). A popup-state case sets
  `viewportOnly: true` and captures the viewport crop.
- **"Ready" is not `networkidle`.** The pages settle their async work into
  observable state — the footer version popup's text, the search placeholder's
  show count. Wait on those (`case-helpers.js`), plus `document.fonts.ready`.
- **Hover-driven UI must be opened inside `capture()`, not `drive()`.** The
  runner settles the scroll between the two, and scrolling moves an element out
  from under the pointer — which fires `mouseleave` and closes anything the
  hover opened. That is correct product behaviour; the capture just has to
  happen on the right side of it.

## The fixture freeze

- `shared/fixtures/data/` is a snapshot of the **real committed data**, cast by
  the committed builder for state variety (sold-out / free / price-unknown /
  tight / every planner verdict). It is **frozen**: the nightly data refresh
  never touches it, and no case may reach for `data/` live files.
- Every deviation from the source bytes is documented as an `ADJUST` in the
  builder — a fixture edit without one is hand-invented data.
- Re-running the builder re-casts every golden. That is a re-baselining: run it
  only with the owner's approval, and land builder + fixtures + goldens +
  gallery in one reviewed change.

## Golden approval, concretely

- A red screen case is **never** fixed by `refresh:ui`. Surface the committed
  golden, `shared/.artifacts/<case>.actual.png` and `.diff.png`, and ask the
  owner (AskUserQuestion popup, per-item, per the owner's preferences) before
  re-baselining anything.
- A brand-new leaf's golden is a **proposal** until the owner has seen the
  rendering: it lands in the PR diff, and merge approval is the pixel
  approval. Say so in the PR body — the goldens are the review surface.
- An intended UI change lands as: spec edit (doc-first, red) → implementation →
  `npm run refresh:ui` → the refreshed PNGs ride the same diff.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **When there's nothing left to do, say so boldly at the end of the conversation.** Don't bury a "this is complete / I'm blocked / nothing further to do" behind hedging — make the terminal state unmistakable. **Set it apart visually so it catches the eye:** put the terminal state — or, when work remains, the list of open/outstanding items — in its own callout (a Markdown blockquote box, e.g. `> ✅ All done` or `> ⚠️ Still open: …`), not trailing prose the owner has to scan for. One or the other always gets the box: the done-signal when nothing remains, the open-items list when something does.
- **"LGTM"** is the owner's phrase for the merge-to-main command: it asks for the change in front of the owner to be merged into `main`. It's an owner-triggered command; the default mechanics live in the `merge-to-main` skill ([merge-to-main/SKILL.md](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md)) (squash, gate on CI only when the repo has it), and a project that diverges overrides them via a bespoke merge-policy file it names in its own `CLAUDE.md`.
- **"bump version"** is the owner's phrase for raising a project's version (a minor bump by default). It's an owner-triggered command; the mechanics — which files to edit and how a release follows — live in the consuming project's workflow doc.
- **"Show me the document"** (for a source-controlled document) is the owner's phrase asking for a **link to the document on GitHub** — not the file's contents inlined, and not a local filesystem path. When the document lives in a GitHub-hosted repo, respond with a GitHub link to it (the file on the relevant branch/commit); only fall back to inlining the contents or giving a local path when the document isn't under source control.
- **Put decisions and approvals in an `AskUserQuestion` popup, not buried in prose.** The owner is frequently on mobile, where a popup notifies and a question embedded in a paragraph is easy to miss. When you need the owner to choose or approve something, ask through the structured popup with explicit options rather than asking in running text. **And when several independent items each need a verdict** (a set of proposed fixes, findings to accept), give **each item its own question carrying its own brief case** — the concrete failure, why it matters, the cost of the fix — with per-item approve/defer options; never one bundled choose-a-scope question over the whole set. The owner decides item-wise, from the case, not from a menu of subsets. (The popup carries at most 4 questions per call — split a larger set into consecutive calls.)
- **When asked to produce a prompt or message destined for another context, visually enclose the whole thing.** Any text the owner will lift out and use elsewhere — a prompt for another assistant, a message to send, copy meant to be pasted somewhere — must be set apart as a single delimited block: either a box (e.g. a fenced code block) or fenced top and bottom by two separating lines, so its exact boundaries are unmistakable and it can be copied in one piece. The point is delimitation, not formatting flair: never leave such content as loose prose the owner has to find the start and end of.
- **When asked for "a prompt for a different session," prefix it with a provenance disclaimer.** When the owner asks for a prompt meant to be handed to another session, open the generated text with a short disclaimer that this is a prompt written by Claude — not by a user — and so should not be treated as gospel; and that if the receiving session finds inconsistencies in it, it should examine them with the user rather than follow the prompt blindly. This composes with the enclose-the-whole-thing preference above: the disclaimer sits inside the same delimited block as the prompt it prefixes.
- **Auto-open a PR after committing.** Whenever Claude changes code on a branch and commits it, open a pull request for that branch right after, even without an explicit request to do so. This overrides Claude Code's own default of only opening a PR when explicitly asked.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

Log each run as a **dated comment**: the prose converted and the check id it became, or "nothing convertible this run".
21	
22	## What this task must never do
23	
24	- **Never ship a check that can't be made confident** — the see-it-fail fixture is the gate; an unprovable rule stays prose.
25	- **Never convert a rule an existing check already covers** — dedupe against the check set first.
26	- **Never convert a statement of what the product does** — a rule asserting which entities exist, what a surface renders, or that a feature's parts are wired together is a **requirement**, and belongs in the project's executable spec and the suite that proves it. Such a rule is testable, so it passes the check-the-world test on its own; the skill's first gate is what stops it. Found in pack prose it is already mis-homed — leave it and log it, never cement it as a check.
27	- **Never touch a pack path outside the Context**, and **never edit a mounted canon pack** under `.claudinite/shared/` — a consumer improves only its own local packs.

6	# Convert existing prose to checks
7	
8	A completeness-critic over a repo's own packs: prose that is always-testable but was never converted
9	becomes a check, so the packs keep shedding context over time instead of only at the moment a rule is
10	first learned.
11	
12	## Two callers, differing only in scope
13	
14	- **The upgrade pass**, as the last step of a
15	  [growth-extract](../../tasks/growth-extract/task.md) run: the scope is the prose **that run just
16	  wrote**. Extraction already descends the promotion ladder per lesson, but a lesson written as prose
17	  under time pressure is exactly where a convertible rule hides, so it gets asked once more before the
18	  PR opens. Never widen from here into the standing backlog.
19	- **The weekly [prose-to-checks-sweep](../../tasks/prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md)**: the scope is the
20	  **standing backlog** — everything under the pack paths configured for this repo, which the task
21	  passes in its Context. A consuming repo's own **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/`) by
22	  default — projects don't improve core canon packs — while **Claudinite itself** also sweeps its core
23	  `packs/`. Read the prose under those paths (each pack's `RULES.md`, and any `SKILL.md` beside them).
24	
25	Plus on demand, when someone asks. Either way: never edit a read-only mounted canon pack under
26	`.claudinite/shared/`. Everything below is identical for both callers.
27	
28	## First gate — a working rule, not a product statement
29	
30	Before asking whether a rule is *testable*, ask whether it belongs to a pack at all: **does it govern
31	how we work, or state what the product does?** A pack — canon or local — homes the conventions,
32	gotchas and review discipline that recur across tasks whatever the feature happens to be. A rule
33	asserting which entities exist, what a surface must render, or that a feature's parts are wired to
34	each other is a **requirement**; its home is the project's executable spec and the suite that proves
35	it (the full rule lives in
36	[generate-project-instructions](../generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md)).
37	
38	This gate comes **first** because product statements sail through the check-the-world test below —
39	"this module must export `X`" has an obvious static signature. Converting one splits a feature's
40	definition across two systems and lands half of it in the one no test of the product ever reads.
41	Load-bearingness is not the test: a real gap in product coverage is a *requirements* gap.
42	
43	A product statement already sitting in pack prose is mis-homed, and a sweep is not the place to
44	re-home it. **Leave the prose and log it** as a mis-homed rule, the same way an un-checkable
45	candidate is logged — never cement it as a check.
46	
47	## What to look for — the check-the-world test
48	
49	For each rule that cleared the gate, ask the one question from
50	[engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md): **does it constrain a *static
51	signature in the repo artifact* — something a post-hoc scan could observe?**
52	
53	- **Yes → a conversion candidate.** A dangling-reference rule, a filename convention, a workflow
54	  or manifest shape, a "these two files must agree" invariant, a forbidden pattern in code.
55	- **No → leave it.** In-flight process (leaves no artifact — "see the test fail first"),
56	  judgment ("name by scope"), or knowledge whose failure is only visible at runtime (jsdom
57	  diverging from Chrome). These are why the rule is prose; don't force them.
58	
59	**A static signature is necessary, not sufficient.** Both shapes the working-discipline rules bar
60	— a rule that pins today's code in place, and one derivable from the product's requirements —
61	answer *yes* here, so screen every candidate against that bar before converting it. Leave either
62	where it is; routing a requirement to the spec and its suite is its own change, not this sweep's.
63	
64	The check-the-world rule from DESIGN holds: if a rule is always-testable, it was never really
65	part of the on-demand skill — it belongs in a pack as a check.
66	
67	## How to convert one
68	
69	Follow the extract stage's check-authoring discipline (the local promotion ladder in
70	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). For each candidate:
71	
72	> **The upgrade-pass caller lands inside growth-extract's own PR**, which auto-merges after CI — so the
73	> see-it-fail fixture is the only gate a converted check gets there. Convert only what you can prove;
74	> anything shakier stays prose and waits for the weekly sweep's reviewed PR.
75	
76	1. **Author the check** in the owning pack (`<pack>/<rule>.mjs`, listed in its `pack.mjs`) — the
77	   failure message *is* the rule (what / why / fix / `doc:` pointer back to the prose).
78	2. **Write the fixture first and see it fail** — a violating fixture must find, a clean one must
79	   not (the test lives beside the pack's other tests). A conversion with no proving fixture
80	   doesn't ship.
81	3. **Ship at real severity, fail-fast** — blocking for a defect, advisory only when the rule is
82	   directional by kind.
83	4. **Delete the prose the check now covers** — whole, never trimmed. The deletion test below is
84	   how you decide which paragraphs those are.
85	
86	**Before writing a rule off as un-checkable, try parsing the file's structure instead of grepping
87	its text.** Grep finds the pattern anywhere; parsing finds it in the one spot the rule means —
88	which kills the false alarm. (Example: `Authorization` is only wrong inside a CloudFront policy's
89	*own* header list, not elsewhere in the template.) Parse only as much as you need, and hold the
90	check to the same fixture bar.
91	
92	When even a scoped parser can't make detection confident, **leave the prose and log the
93	candidate** to a tagged conversion-backlog issue rather than shipping a shaky check.
94	
95	## Coming out: the deletion test
96	
97	Coming out of a conversion, apply the **deletion test**: prose a mechanism fully covers is
98	deleted, never trimmed. Ask it of every paragraph standing beside a landed check — *with this
99	paragraph gone, would the check still catch every violation it describes **and** tell the agent
100	how to fix it?* If yes, it is redundant: delete it whole. The check's failure message is where
101	the rule lives now and its header comment is where the rationale lives, so a paragraph restating
102	either pays twice and is the drift trap waiting to spring.
103	
104	Before concluding prose is the only carrier, look at the pack's **skills** too — an
105	activity-scoped skill often already holds the map a rule is repeating. Keep only what no artifact
106	carries.
107	
108	The test **discriminates** rather than just deleting: a paragraph stays whole whenever it carries
109	something the check does not — a second rule in the same breath, an exemption the check can't
110	encode, a value the check can't judge, or a remedy the finding's own `fix` line never states
111	(a finding renders `what` / `why` / `fix` / `doc`, never the rule's `description`, so a remedy
112	that lives only in the description is not carried). Two worked calls: an `npm test` invariant
113	went entirely — the check caught it and the testing-guide skill already listed the suites —
114	while an `extension-test/` mirror bullet stayed, because the check beside it enforced only the
115	`package.json` list's sync with the tree and never the mirror convention itself.
116	
117	Whether a check covers a rule is a judgment about meaning, so this test is applied by a
118	**reader**, not mechanized.
119	
120	## Bounds
121	
122	- **One PR, bounded surface** — the new rule module, its `pack.mjs` line, its fixture, and the
123	  trimmed prose. Don't "improve" unrelated rules while you're in there.
124	- **Never delete a rule you didn't convert** — the deletion test is only ever asked of a rule a
125	  *landed* check now enforces.
126	- Run the suite and the sweep green before the PR goes up, and never push to `main` directly. The
127	  sweep opens its own PR for the owner's approval; the upgrade pass adds its conversion to the
128	  growth-extract PR already being opened, and opens none of its own.

1	# edfringe-requirements — the executable-requirements harness here
2	
3	How this repo runs its spec (`product/requirements.md`) as tests. The framework
4	conventions are the `executable-requirements` pack; the judgment layer is
5	`spec-driven-product` + the `writing-tests` skill. This pack carries only what
6	those don't: the mechanics of a **real-headless-browser** golden harness (the
7	canon's worked examples render with satori/jsdom or Flutter — this repo is the
8	first Playwright port) and the local approval/fixture policy. Layout, lanes and
9	commands live in [product/requirements/README.md](../../../../product/requirements/README.md)
10	— don't restate them; this file is the judgment and the traps.
11	
12	## The document reads as pictures
13	
14	- `product/requirements.md` is scanned by sight: under each visual leaf its
15	  golden is **visible, uncollapsed**; every textual expansion (acceptance
16	  notes, proof pointers) is **collapsed** in a `<details>` block. An optimal
17	  requirements document has almost no words on the page.
18	- **A visual leaf's statement is a line, not a paragraph.** The golden already
19	  carries the exact copy, counts, colours and placement — restating them in
20	  prose only competes with the picture. Say what is being asserted; let the
21	  image say how it looks. Anything genuinely not visible (a threshold, a rule
22	  behind the state, a condition that produced it) goes in a collapsed
23	  **Notes** block, never in the statement.
24	- **A golden is the smallest surface that proves its leaf** — an element crop,
25	  a clipped region, or a stitched composite (e.g. one grid lane narrowed to a
26	  few days, recomposed with its label and verdict columns, no header) — never
27	  the whole page or even the whole control. The capture recipe lives on the
28	  case (`capture: "<selector>"` or `capture(page, tools)`; see
29	  `shared/capture-tools.js`); whole-page capture is a deliberate exception,
30	  not a default. Scoping is judgment: crop to what the leaf asserts, keep just
31	  enough surroundings to orient.
32	- **A change over time is an animation, not a coded assertion.** When a
33	  requirement is about what an action *changes* — a dismissal that sticks, a
34	  pick that swaps one card for another — capture the same region before and
35	  after (and after a reload, where persistence is the point) and play the
36	  frames as one animated golden (`tools.animate`). A flow is shown as a flow.
37	  Reserve `stitchV`/`stitchH` for things that are genuinely side by side rather
38	  than sequential.
39	- **An animated golden is an APNG, never a GIF** — the choice
40	  ShoutsAndWhispers made for its sagas, for two reasons that both matter here:
41	  APNG is lossless, so the golden stays a faithful pixel record of the UI
42	  instead of a 256-colour approximation of it, and every byte is ours, so the
43	  comparison stays exact byte-identity. It animates in GitHub markdown exactly
44	  like a GIF. The encoder is `shared/png.js`'s `encodeAnimated`; the comparator
45	  detects an animated golden and compares bytes only, since a pixel differ
46	  reads one still frame and would describe the wrong thing.
47	
48	## A requirement is a feature, not a module
49	
50	The spec is organised by what the product *does*, never by how the code is
51	arranged. "Shared code" is not a requirement category: a rule both front-ends
52	follow is one feature, and its picture shows **both** the Now page and the
53	planner — a rule only half the site follows is not the feature. Those
54	cross-page features sit in their own part **after** the two page-by-page
55	segments, so each page reads as a whole first.
56	
57	Cross-page proof is ordinary: a case may navigate between the pages (or open a
58	second page, when something fixed at context creation — a device timezone —
59	has to differ) and stitch or animate the surfaces into one golden.
60	
61	## Prefer several pictures over one coded leaf
62	
63	Before routing a leaf to `behavior` or `logic`, ask whether it **decomposes
64	into observable states**. A statement joined by "and" usually does, and each
65	part is then its own numbered sub-leaf with its own picture — the parent
66	becomes a heading. The time wheel went this way: "5-minute steps, opens at
67	now + 2 h, ends at 29:55" was one coded leaf and is now `3.7.1`–`3.7.3`, three
68	crops anyone can check by eye. Sub-leaves are cheap; a coded assertion the
69	owner has to read code to trust is not.
70	
71	Reserve the coded kinds for what genuinely has no picture:
72	
73	- **`behavior`** — a gesture's outgoing consequence (a URL built, bytes
74	  downloaded, storage written), or a fact the OS paints rather than the page
75	  (a native `title` tooltip, a cursor — neither can appear in a screenshot).
76	- **`logic`** — a pure rule with no rendered surface at all. When the rule is
77	  about *how values are written*, prefer a **table** over prose: a case may
78	  declare `table: { columns, rows }`, the gallery renders it into the spec, and
79	  its `verify()` proves every row against the shipped code — so the table a
80	  reader sees is generated evidence, not a hand-typed claim.
81	
82	When a leaf lands in a coded kind *because* the product makes it invisible,
83	say so in its Notes and name what product change would make it visual — that
84	is a real finding about the UI, not just a testing limitation.
85	
86	## The browser is part of the expected
87	
88	- A golden is only comparable under the **exact Chromium that rendered it**.
89	  The harness pins the Playwright version and refuses any other
90	  (`shared/harness/browser.js`); CI installs that pin per run, the Claude
91	  sandbox ships it globally. **Bumping the pin re-renders every golden** — it
92	  is a re-baselining, done deliberately and approved like one, never a drive-by
93	  upgrade.
94	- When the comparison ever flaps, the fix is **more determinism, not a
95	  tolerance**: the comparator stays at zero diff. The determinism levers are
96	  all in one place (the harness): fixed clock via `page.clock`, fixed
97	  geolocation, seeded `Math.random`, route-fulfilled network, frozen
98	  animations, `--font-render-hinting=none --force-color-profile=srgb`.
99	
100	## Traps this harness already paid for (don't re-derive)
101	
102	- **Geolocation exists only on secure origins.** The fake origin is `https://`
103	  — route interception fulfils before any TLS, so no certificate is involved.
104	  On plain http the app silently keeps its built-in simulated clock and the
105	  whole render lands on the wrong day.
106	- **The app adopts the device clock only on an in-UK geolocation fix** — the
107	  harness's fixed location is central Edinburgh precisely so the pinned clock
108	  is what renders; deny geolocation (or move abroad) and you are rendering the
109	  app's own pre-set simulated moment instead, a different day file entirely.
110	- **A CSS freeze does not stop Web-Animations-API animations.** The planner's
111	  FLIP board diff runs through `element.animate` — the harness stubs it to
112	  land on end states; without the stub, captures race the animation.
113	- **Fonts arrive via the Google Fonts CSS URL**, so the vendored `fonts.css`'s
114	  `url(/__vendor/…)` references resolve against `fonts.googleapis.com` — the
115	  vendor route must match on path, host-agnostic, or every glyph silently
116	  falls back and all text shifts by a pixel.
117	- **Vendoring the web fonts is only half the font problem.** Every character
118	  they don't carry — an emoji, `▾`, `≤`, a Cyrillic show title — is drawn from
119	  the fonts *installed on the machine*, so the goldens quietly become a record
120	  of the renderer's font set. It cost a red CI lane: the walk-time line
121	  (`🚶 5 min · £16`) measured wider on the GitHub runner, wrapped, and every
122	  show card came out 21px taller. The harness now launches Chromium under a
123	  generated `FONTCONFIG_FILE` whose only font directory is
124	  `harness/vendor/systemfonts/` — the host's fonts cannot reach the page. A new
125	  emoji or script in the product or the fixtures needs that subset rebuilt
126	  (see the folder's README), or it renders as tofu.
127	- **A floating popup dies under a full-page screenshot** (the capture scrolls,
128	  and scroll dismisses tips/legends/optimizer pops). A popup-state case sets
129	  `viewportOnly: true` and captures the viewport crop.
130	- **"Ready" is not `networkidle`.** The pages settle their async work into
131	  observable state — the footer version popup's text, the search placeholder's
132	  show count. Wait on those (`case-helpers.js`), plus `document.fonts.ready`.
133	- **Hover-driven UI must be opened inside `capture()`, not `drive()`.** The
134	  runner settles the scroll between the two, and scrolling moves an element out
135	  from under the pointer — which fires `mouseleave` and closes anything the
136	  hover opened. That is correct product behaviour; the capture just has to
137	  happen on the right side of it.
138	
139	## The fixture freeze
140	
141	- `shared/fixtures/data/` is a snapshot of the **real committed data**, cast by
142	  the committed builder for state variety (sold-out / free / price-unknown /
143	  tight / every planner verdict). It is **frozen**: the nightly data refresh
144	  never touches it, and no case may reach for `data/` live files.
145	- Every deviation from the source bytes is documented as an `ADJUST` in the
146	  builder — a fixture edit without one is hand-invented data.
147	- Re-running the builder re-casts every golden. That is a re-baselining: run it
148	  only with the owner's approval, and land builder + fixtures + goldens +
149	  gallery in one reviewed change.
150	
151	## Golden approval, concretely
152	
153	- A red screen case is **never** fixed by `refresh:ui`. Surface the committed
154	  golden, `shared/.artifacts/<case>.actual.png` and `.diff.png`, and ask the
155	  owner (AskUserQuestion popup, per-item, per the owner's preferences) before
156	  re-baselining anything.
157	- A brand-new leaf's golden is a **proposal** until the owner has seen the
158	  rendering: it lands in the PR diff, and merge approval is the pixel
159	  approval. Say so in the PR body — the goldens are the review surface.
160	- An intended UI change lands as: spec edit (doc-first, red) → implementation →
161	  `npm run refresh:ui` → the refreshed PNGs ride the same diff.

1	# EdFringeNow — project working rules
2	
3	Lessons captured while working in this repo, layered on the shared Claudinite
4	canon. Terse and concrete; read the matching one before working in that area.
5	
6	## The owner asks in plain words — open the issue yourself, before the first commit
7	
8	Work here arrives as a chat request ("Maybe we can just put a 'Show list/Show Map'
9	toggle selector just under the filter…"), never as a filed issue. The
10	`task-lifecycle` check still wants a commit on the branch to reference one, so
11	**open the issue as your first step and put `Closes #N` in the original commit
12	message** — write it from the owner's own words, since it is the only record of
13	what was asked.
14	
15	Leaving it to the stop hook is the expensive path, and it is the path every
16	session took: 7 of the 12 sessions captured on 2026-07-29 declared the work done,
17	got blocked, and then paid create-issue + `git commit --amend` +
18	`git push --force-with-lease` + a second reply that added nothing (#134 33s,
19	#150 45s, #152 35s, #154 43s, #156 43s, #158 57s, #160 20s — ~4.6 min of pure
20	rework). Worse, by then the PR is already open, so the fix rewrites the commit
21	underneath it.
22	
23	## A dispatched run still has to classify its trigger comment
24	
25	The `comment-classification` check reads the last message addressed to you and
26	wants a `Comment class:` line in the reply to it. In a scheduled run that message
27	is the executor prompt ("Execute the Claudinite executor: …"), not anything the
28	owner wrote — but the check does not distinguish them, and it is BLOCKING at the
29	Stop hook. 19 of the sessions captured across 2026-07-29…07-31 were stopped by
30	exactly this finding, every one of them citing the dispatch prompt, and each paid
31	an extra closing reply to clear it (the two runs where the block lands at the end
32	and the cost is cleanly isolable: #183 115s, #160 121s).
33	
34	So **close a dispatched run's final reply with an explicit `Comment class:` line
35	classifying the dispatch itself** — `process-change` for an executor/scheduled-task
36	prompt — instead of discovering the requirement at Stop. On a real owner comment
37	the classification is the substance; on a dispatch it is a formality, but it is
38	far cheaper paid up front than as a second reply.
39	
40	## Read the PR's state, then merge — never loop on `enable_pr_auto_merge`
41	
42	`mcp__github__enable_pr_auto_merge` only accepts a PR whose required checks are
43	still **pending**. This repo's `ci.yml` runs on `pull_request` and finishes in
44	well under a minute, so by the time an agent reaches the arming step the PR is
45	usually already `clean` and the call errors — *"already in clean status (all
46	checks passed) … you can merge directly."* That is not a failure to work around:
47	take it as the answer and call `mcp__github__merge_pull_request` with `SQUASH`.
48	
49	The other refusal, *"in unstable status (required checks are failing)"*, is not a
50	verdict either — a check that is queued, or held at the Actions approval gate,
51	reads identically to one that failed. Re-read the PR
52	(`mcp__github__pull_request_read`) or the run list (`mcp__github__actions_list`)
53	to find out which, and never re-arm on a loop: PR #188 answered "unstable" and
54	then "clean" 27s later with nothing changed in between, and PR #182 answered
55	"unstable" three times across ~4 minutes before answering "clean".
56	
57	The cost is measured. The 2026-08-01 baselining run spent ~350s of its 765s — 4
58	arm attempts, 9 `pull_request_read`s and 5 `ScheduleWakeup` polls — circling PR
59	#182's merge state, and still ended without merging it; the owner merged it by
60	hand the next evening. The same morning's conversation-extract run took its one
61	refusal as an answer and squash-merged 22s later. Check state first, merge
62	directly when it is clean, and arm auto-merge only while checks are genuinely
63	pending.
64	
65	## Verifying UI changes visually (the `index.html` page and everything under `plan/`)
66	
67	Visual verification of the pages **is** available in this sandbox. Don't skip it
68	or downgrade to "verified by logic review only" claiming no browser exists — a
69	browser is here, and a UI change isn't done until it has been looked at.
70	
71	- Serve the repo and drive it with the preinstalled Chromium (or Playwright):
72	  `python3 -m http.server 8000`, then screenshot / click through
73	  `http://localhost:8000`. The app fetches `data/shows.json`, so it must be
74	  served over HTTP rather than opened as a file — and `localhost` bypasses the
75	  agent proxy, so the browser reaches the page even though external hosts need
76	  the proxy.
77	- **Launch Playwright with no `executablePath`, and import from `index.mjs`.**
78	  `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=/opt/pw-browsers` is already exported in this
79	  sandbox, so `chromium.launch()` finds its browser on its own. Import the
80	  global build by its ESM entry —
81	  `import { chromium } from '/opt/node22/lib/node_modules/playwright/index.mjs'`
82	  (the sibling `index.js` is CJS, so a *named* import from it yields
83	  `undefined`) — or `$(npm root -g)/playwright/index.mjs` if the prefix moved.
84	  Path discovery and its sed-fix-up round-trips cost ~220s across five captured
85	  sessions, every one of them re-deriving the same two facts.
86	  `/opt/pw-browsers/chromium` is a **symlink** onto the version-pinned
87	  `chromium-<build>/chrome-linux/chrome`, so it is a valid `executablePath` if
88	  you ever need one — but you don't, and the build it points at moves with the
89	  image.
90	- **Never `npm i playwright` into the scratchpad to make the import resolve.**
91	  A bare `import { chromium } from 'playwright'` in a scratchpad script fails
92	  with `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` — the global install is not on the resolution
93	  path, and `NODE_PATH` does not apply to ESM, so exporting it changes nothing.
94	  The obvious next move is the wrong one: a fresh `npm i playwright` pulls a
95	  **newer** Playwright than the image's, which then hunts for a browser build
96	  the image does not ship (`chromium_headless_shell-1234` against the vendored
97	  `-1194`) and dies asking for `npx playwright install` — a download the
98	  sandbox cannot make. Three sessions on 2026-08-07 (#251, #258, #264) each
99	  took that detour and then backed out of it. Use the absolute path to the
100	  global build instead: it is the one matched to the vendored browsers.
101	- To build a `/plan` favourites list for the render, a plain slug-per-line text
102	  file is accepted by the parser — pick shows spanning the statuses (and some
103	  same-day doubles) you want to eyeball.
104	- **Known-noisy console output from the served page.** A page driven off
105	  `python3 -m http.server` reliably logs a `favicon.ico` 404 (the repo ships
106	  none) and often `net::ERR_CONNECTION_RESET` as the browser tears down. Neither
107	  is an application error — filter both out of a smoke script's error assertion
108	  so that a red run means something, rather than sending you chasing a phantom
109	  404 through extra browser runs.
110	- To match edfringe.com's live styling (e.g. the ticket-availability colours on
111	  the `/plan` grid), fetch the official site's CSS with `curl` through the agent
112	  proxy and read the palette out of it. `WebFetch` returns rendered text without
113	  the CSS, and headless Chromium cannot tunnel the proxy to reach an external
114	  host — `curl` is the one path that works for off-box assets.
115	
116	## The live site is reachable — check real state at `*.edfringenow.com`, allowing for CDN lag
117	
118	The environment's egress policy allows `*.edfringenow.com`, the live site's own
119	domain. So a question about what the deployed site actually serves — is the new
120	field in `data/shows.json`? did the deploy land? — is answerable directly, with
121	`curl https://www.edfringenow.com/…` through the agent proxy, rather than by
122	reasoning from the working tree. General egress is still closed: everything
123	*except* the allowed domain fails the same way, so this is a single-domain
124	window, not open internet.
125	
126	Two caveats before you trust what comes back:
127	
128	- **The response is CDN-cached, so a fresh push may not be visible yet.** A
129	  200 with stale content is not evidence the deploy failed — re-check after a
130	  delay, and never conclude "the change didn't ship" from one read taken
131	  seconds after the push.
132	- **Confirm the allowance is live in *your* session before relying on it.** The
133	  policy is per-environment and a session can be running under an older one; on
134	  2026-08-07 a probe of both `www.edfringenow.com` and the apex returned
135	  `curl: (56) CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403`. A 403 at CONNECT is a policy
136	  denial, not a site outage — `curl -sS "$HTTPS_PROXY/__agentproxy/status"`
137	  lists the recent rejections and confirms which it is. When it's denied, say so
138	  and fall back to the repo, rather than reporting the live site as down.
139	
140	As with the off-box CSS fetch above, `curl` is the working path: headless
141	Chromium cannot tunnel the proxy, and `WebFetch` returns rendered text rather
142	than the raw JSON or asset you usually want here.
143	
144	## Watching a workflow or scheduler run — never a blind fixed sleep
145	
146	If the run is still going, ask again. On 2026-08-07 #251 abandoned its poll and
147	fell back to a blind `sleep 90` — for a run `actions_get` reported *already
148	complete* five seconds later. The orphaned sleep then fired two
149	`task-notification`s that had to be explained away to the owner.
150	
151	## The site is two front-ends — cross-page behaviour goes in `shared/`
152	
153	The Now page (`index.html` + `js/app.js`) and the planner (`plan/` + `plan/plan.js`)
154	are separate front-ends, and `plan/lib/` is the planner's own engine, not a common
155	library. But both are now ES modules, so **anything that must behave the same on
156	both pages belongs in `shared/`** and is imported by each — never copy-pasted.
157	Both pages spell the import the same way (`../shared/geo.js` resolves to
158	`/shared/geo.js` from either), so moving a value there is a small change.
159	
160	What is still genuinely twinned (untangled the same way when next touched): the
161	header `debug v<version>` pill, the Now/Plan nav, and the haversine in
162	`plan/lib/travel.js` that was ported from `js/app.js`.
163	
164	A shared module needs **no** `package.json` to mark it as ESM: the pinned Node 22
165	detects module syntax in a `.js` file by itself, with no warning and no flag, so
166	`node --check` and the test suite both handle it. `plan/package.json` predates
167	that detection and its stated reason (silencing a module-detection warning) no
168	longer applies; it is harmless, so it stays, but do not copy it as a pattern —
169	the `edfringe-no-stray-package-json` check flags any other one.
170	`.js` and `.mjs` are both served as `text/javascript` by `python3 -m http.server`,
171	so the extension is a style choice — use `.js`, matching `plan/lib/`.
172	
173	A new top-level source dir must be added to `scripts/verify.sh`'s `git ls-files`
174	list, or nothing in it is ever parse-checked — the `edfringe-verify-sh-covers-source-dirs`
175	check catches an omission.
176	
177	## `.claudinite/shared/` is generated output — never hand-resolve its conflicts, always take the fresher version
178	
179	## A pack rule or check encodes a *work procedure*, never product behaviour
180	
181	Rules and checks in `.claudinite/local/packs/` are about **how work is done here**
182	— the gate that must stay wired, the tool that must be launched a certain way, the
183	files that must move together. **Product behaviour is not a rule.** What the site
184	does — which ticket statuses count as unavailable, what the Now page shows, how
185	far "walkable" reaches — is a **requirement**, and it belongs in the requirements
186	spec (`product/requirements.md`, the `executable-requirements` pack) and its
187	tests, never in a pack's `rules`.
188	
189	The trap is that product behaviour reads exactly like a good check candidate: it
190	is deterministic, statically detectable, and genuinely worth enforcing, so a
191	prose-to-checks sweep will happily convert it. The 2026-07-30 sweep did: it turned
192	the `ticketStatus`-not-`soldOut` rule into an `edfringe-ticket-status-unavailable`
193	check, with a clean scoped parse and a see-it-fail proof against mutated real repo
194	content — a well-built check of the wrong kind, which the owner rejected on sight
195	("Rules shouldn't be about product requirements, only work procedures"). The
196	sibling conversion in the same PR, `edfringe-normalizer-selftest-in-verify` ("the
197	offline self-test must stay wired into `verify.sh`"), was the right kind and
198	stayed.
199	
200	Apply the test **before** writing the check, since the build quality of the check
201	tells you nothing about whether it belongs: *if the product changed its mind
202	tomorrow, would this rule be wrong?* If yes it is a requirement — a red check
203	would then be reporting a product decision as a process violation, and the
204	requirements spec is where that decision is already supposed to live. If instead
205	it would still hold because it describes how we work regardless of what the
206	product does, it is a rule. Prose in a `RULES.md` gets the same test: the
207	`ticketStatus` paragraph in the `edfringe-data` pack is background a scraper
208	editor needs, not a rule, and it is not convertible.
209	
210	## Retiring a practice: delete it, state the rule that replaces it, don't narrate the change
211	
212	When a practice is withdrawn, the docs that taught it get **rewritten into the
213	current rule in the present tense** — not amended with a paragraph explaining what
214	used to be done and why it stopped. The owner's words on PR #240: *"make sure the
215	rules and comments are describing current state, not past changes. Describe the
216	rules, not the history."*
217	
218	The first pass at retiring the `probe-edfringe-api` skill did the opposite, and
219	every part of it read as diligence at the time: the pack `RULES.md`, its `README.md`
220	and `scraper/SCRAPING.md` each gained a passage narrating the retired probe practice
221	so a future reader would understand the ban. All of it came back out on review. A
222	reader who never knew the practice does not need to be taught it in order to be told
223	the rule, and describing it is how a withdrawn technique keeps getting rediscovered.
224	
225	The same pass also added a new `edfringe-workflows-allowlisted` check — every file
226	under `.github/workflows/` had to sit on a named allowlist — built properly, with
227	red-first fixtures and a live gate over the real tree. The owner removed it too:
228	retiring one practice is not the moment to install a guard against it. State the
229	rule; a check earns its place on its own, from a mistake that actually repeats, not
230	as the enforcement arm of the deletion that prompted it.
231	
232	This does **not** ban evidence. The measured costs cited throughout this file are
233	what argue a rule is worth its space, and they stay. What goes is narration of a
234	*superseded* way of working: the rule is what the reader needs, and the history
235	belongs to the commit that removed it.

1	# EdFringeNow — the data pipeline (scraper/ and data/)
2	
3	The domain of this pack: getting show data out of edfringe.com and into the
4	committed files the site serves. Read it before touching `scraper/` or anything
5	under `data/`. The API's own field reference lives in
6	[scraper/SCRAPING.md](../../../../scraper/SCRAPING.md) and the file layout in
7	[scraper/README.md](../../../../scraper/README.md) — this is the working
8	judgment those two don't carry.
9	
10	## The live API is unreachable from a session — don't try, and don't fake it
11	
12	`edfringe-tikketr-web-api.equhost.com` is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy
13	(403 at the CONNECT). So: no session — this one included —
14	can verify a scraper change against live data. Anything that must touch the API
15	runs through a sanctioned workflow: the `Scrape edfringe shows (full)` workflow
16	(`.github/workflows/scrape.yml`), `Fetch ticket prices (one-off)`
17	(`prices.yml`), or the `refresh-shows` / `refresh-tickets` scheduled tasks.
18	Never "verify" a scraper change by reasoning about what the API probably
19	returns — either have a sanctioned workflow run it, or say plainly that it is
20	unverified.
21	
22	The egress block is a **policy boundary, not an obstacle to route around**. Do
23	not create ad-hoc GitHub Actions workflows — push-triggered "probes" or
24	anything else — to reach the API (or any blocked host) from an open-network
25	runner: that is CI as a side channel around the session's network rules.
26	
27	For one-off API questions (a field's shape, an enum's value set, whether an
28	operation exists at all), `scraper/SCRAPING.md` is the reference. When it falls
29	short there is one legitimate source short of asking the owner:
30	**`www.edfringe.com` itself is reachable**, and its Next.js bundles carry the
31	client's complete GraphQL operation set — every query, mutation and fragment,
32	with full field selections. Recipe in SCRAPING.md ("Reaching it from a Claude
33	Code web session"). That is reading a public asset from an allowed host, and it
34	is how the "no bulk price endpoint" claim was finally settled. It tells you what
35	a query would look like, never what it returns — so a change checked only that
36	way is still unverified against live data and must be reported as such. If that
37	doesn't answer it either, ask the repo owner rather than building a bypass.
38	
39	`python3 scraper/normalize.py --selftest` is the one transform check that runs
40	offline; it exercises raw→master→day-file→`shows.min.json` on a fixture, so a
41	normalizer change is verifiable here even though a fetch change is not. Because
42	it is the only offline verification a scraper change can get, it must stay wired
43	into `scripts/verify.sh` — the `edfringe-normalizer-selftest-in-verify` check
44	enforces that (a step *label* naming the self-test does not count; only a command
45	line does).
46	
47	## `ticketStatus`, never the `soldOut` boolean
48	
49	"Can I get a ticket" comes from the per-performance `ticketStatus`, not the
50	`soldOut` flag: a performance can be `soldOut: false` and still have nothing to
51	sell online (`NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE`). The site treats `SOLD_OUT` and
52	`NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` as unavailable and everything else as available
53	(`NO_TICKETS_STATUSES` in `js/app.js`), and unknown means available. Any new
54	availability logic — client or scraper — keys off `ticketStatus`; `soldOut` is
55	carried through for display only.
56	
57	## A price belongs to a performance, not to a show
58	
59	The same run sells at several prices: previews cheaper than the main run,
60	weekends dearer than weekdays. The first price pass didn't know that — it
61	called `performancePrices` for **one** performance per show and filed the answer
62	under the show. Pre-festival the performance it picked was almost always the
63	earliest, i.e. a preview, so **1,016 of 3,664 priced shows (28%) published their
64	cheapest night as their price**: Alfie Brown's £15/£16 run shipped as £8.50.
65	
66	The fix is not a rule about previews, and adding a "skip previews" or
67	"price after date X" heuristic re-creates the same class of bug from a different
68	angle — it still picks one performance and hopes it represents the rest.
69	**Price every performance.** There is no bulk price *field*, but GraphQL aliases
70	make one request carry a whole show's run (`fetch_prices.prices_query`), so full
71	per-night pricing costs roughly the same ~3,700 requests as the old pass. There
72	is no call budget to economise against here, so don't design as if there were.
73	
74	Which payload gets which number is the load-bearing distinction:
75	
76	| payload | question it answers | price |
77	|---|---|---|
78	| master, `shows.min.json` (planner) | what does this *show* cost? | run-wide `priceMin`..`priceMax` |
79	| `data/days/*.json` (Now page) | what does it cost *tonight*? | that performance's own `pm` |
80	
81	A performance the cache has no entry for gets **no `pm` at all** — "Price TBC" —
82	rather than the show's minimum. Borrowing a neighbouring night's figure is
83	exactly the bug above, and a lower bound presented as the price is a lie about
84	money even when every number in it is real.
85	
86	## Prices are fetched once, and "unknown" is a third state the encoding must keep
87	
88	`data/prices.json` is a fetch-once cache (`scraper/fetch_prices.py`), off the
89	nightly path: a show's price bands are set when it goes on sale, unlike its
90	ticket status. `refresh-shows` reads the cache and carries the amounts through
91	untouched — it never re-fetches them. So the festival keeps adding shows the
92	cache has never seen, and **a show with no price is a normal, permanent state of
93	the data**, not a gap the pipeline should close.
94	
95	The cache carries two entry shapes and both must stay readable: current entries
96	have `sets` + `perfs` (per performance), and entries from the old pass have a
97	bare whole-show `min`/`max`. The migration completes one show per re-run, so
98	dropping the legacy shape — or emptying the cache to "start clean" — would blank
99	every price on the site until a full pass finished. `price_sets` reads both.
100	
101	Which means the encoding carries three states, not two, and every stage has to
102	preserve the distinction:
103	
104	| state | master | wire |
105	|---|---|---|
106	| costs nothing | `priceMin: 0` | `pm: 0` |
107	| priced | `priceMin: 22.5` | `pm: 22.5` |
108	| unknown | `priceMin: null` | no `pm` key at all |
109	
110	`priceMin: 0` and `free: true` are **not** the same claim and don't always agree.
111	The flag comes from the listing; the £0 can also come from the price API, which
112	returns a single `Price band 1` at £0.00 for a handful of shows the listing
113	doesn't flag free — pay-what-you-want, or a box office that never set a price
114	(10 of 3,664 in the first full run). Both readings are honest about what a ticket
115	costs, so the price path keys off `priceMin`, and `free` stays what the *listing*
116	said. Don't "fix" one to match the other.
117	
118	Never encode unknown as `0`, and never let a decoder default it to one: a stage
119	that collapses three states into two is lying about money, and nothing
120	downstream can recover the difference. What the site then *does* with an unknown
121	price is a product decision, not a pipeline one — it lives in `shared/price.js`.
122	
123	Two traps in the raw price payload, both already handled and both worth not
124	re-introducing: amounts arrive as **strings**, and nearly every show carries a
125	£0.00 "Personal Assistant" concession (a carer's companion ticket) that must not
126	be read as the cheapest price. See the pricing section of
127	[scraper/SCRAPING.md](../../../../scraper/SCRAPING.md).
128	
129	## The API stamps performances in UTC — cross the zone once, at the edge
130	
131	The listing API's `dateTime` is a real UTC instant (`"2026-08-06T11:45:00.000Z"`),
132	**not** Edinburgh wall-clock with a decorative `Z`. Slicing the digits out of that
133	string is the trap: it looks like it works — every date and time in it is
134	plausible — and in August it is silently an hour wrong for the whole catalogue.
135	That is exactly what shipped, and what #275 cost to undo: 60,115 performances
136	listed an hour early, with the tell being shows that name their own time (a 10am
137	"Shakespeare for Breakfast" sitting at 09:00).
138	
139	The pipeline has **one** time-zone crossing, and it is `normalize.local_date_start`.
140	`refresh_ticket_status.py` and `fetch_prices.py` share it so a performance is keyed
141	by the same local date and start everywhere. Everything written after it — the
142	master, `data/days/*.json`, `availability.min.json`, `shows.min.json` — is already
143	Edinburgh wall-clock, so **no stage downstream parses, converts, or re-offsets a
144	time**. Treating a stored value as UTC a second time is the same bug from the other
145	end.
146	
147	Two consequences to hold on to when touching this:
148	
149	- **A "now" compared against these times is read in Edinburgh too** — `js/clock.js`
150	  (`festivalNow` / `festivalDate`), never the device clock. A UK visitor cannot see
151	  the difference, which is why a device clock survives review; a visitor planning
152	  from another zone reintroduces the whole drift.
153	- **A conversion change is a full-snapshot change.** The committed data is generator
154	  output, so the fix is not complete until the master is rebuilt through the new
155	  conversion and every derived artifact regenerated from it. Shifting the boundary
156	  moves performances between day files (two late 31 Aug performances now fall into
157	  1 Sep, outside the August day files, and live only in the master and the planner's
158	  catalogue) — expect that and check it, rather than reading it as data loss.
159	
160	## The committed data is generated output — regenerate it, never hand-edit it
161	
162	`data/raw_pages/` is a git-ignored regenerable cache. `data/normalized/`,
163	`data/venues.json` and `data/days/` **are** committed, because the browser
164	fetches them — but they are still generator output. Fix the data by fixing
165	`scraper/normalize.py` and re-running it (`--merge` for a top-up, no flag for a
166	full rebuild from the raw cache); a hand-edit is silently overwritten by the next
167	`refresh-shows` run and leaves the bug in the generator.
168	
169	`data/prices.json` is the one exception, and it is an exception to the *direction*
170	rather than the rule: it is committed, but it is normalize.py's **input**, written
171	by `scraper/fetch_prices.py`. Nothing regenerates it on a schedule, so nothing
172	overwrites a hand-edit either — which is precisely why editing it by hand is still
173	wrong: the edit survives, silently disagreeing with the box office forever. Re-run
174	the fetch. The `edfringe-data-dir-is-generator-output` check allows it **by name**,
175	so a second file can't ride in on its shape.
176	
177	## Changing the wire format is a four-file change
178	
179	The day files and `shows.min.json` reference `data/venues.json`'s global lists
180	**by position** (`genre`, `room`, `subs`, `ts`; `g`, `rm`, `sg`, `ar`). That
181	encoding has one producer and two decoders, and they must move together:
182	
183	- producer — `scraper/normalize.py` (`build_lookups` / `build_day_files` /
184	  `minify_master` / `build_availability`)
185	- decoder 1 — `js/app.js` `adaptShow`, for the day files
186	- decoder 2 — `plan/lib/hydrate.js` `rehydrateShows`, the exact inverse of
187	  `minify_master`, round-tripped against the real committed files by
188	  `plan/lib/__tests__/hydrate.test.mjs`
189	
190	Add or drop an indexed field and all three change in the same commit. That the
191	indices still *resolve* is enforced by the `edfringe-lookup-indices` check — it
192	catches a lookup list regenerated without its day files, but nothing can catch a
193	decoder left reading the old key, so check both decoders by hand.
194	
195	Two properties of that encoding are load-bearing for caching, and both fail
196	silently:
197	
198	- **The lookup lists are append-only** (`extend_lookup`). The browser holds
199	  `shows.min.json` for four days and `venues.json` for one, so a stale catalogue
200	  is routinely decoded against a newer lookup file. An entry that changed index
201	  would relabel shows' genres and rooms with no error anywhere. Entries are never
202	  dropped, even once the master stops using them.
203	- **`shows.min.json` carries nothing that changes through the day.** Ticket
204	  status lives in `availability.min.json` (its own status list, indexing into
205	  nothing, so the hourly refresh can rewrite it alone). Putting a status back in
206	  the catalogue would restart its hourly churn *and* freeze availability for
207	  anyone holding a cached copy — the bug in #249, re-created from the other end.
208	  `hydrate.test.mjs` asserts each wire performance carries only `d` and `s`.
209	
210	The same three-way move applies to plain (non-indexed) wire keys such as the
211	price fields `pm` / `px`, with one extra hazard: the round-trip test compares the
212	rehydrated record to the master **as JSON**, so a new master key has to appear in
213	the *same position* in `normalize_event`'s dict and in `rehydrateShows`'s object
214	literal. Adding it in one place and appending it in the other fails the
215	round-trip on key order alone, which reads as a data bug and isn't one.
